title: OWASP Top 10 (2021) — The Ten Most Common Web Risks

levels.beginner: Think of a web app as a house. The OWASP Top 10 is a list of the ten ways burglars most often get in: unlocked doors, weak locks, hidden spare keys, and so on. You do not need to memorise every detail yet — just learn what each risk is called and why it matters.
levels.intermediate: Each of the ten categories names a class of weakness, not a single bug. For every category you should be able to say: what the attacker gains, what code pattern causes it, and what the standard defence is. The categories overlap — one real vulnerability often fits two of them.
levels.advanced: Use the Top 10 as a review checklist and a threat-model input, not as a complete security standard. It ranks common, high-impact risks in typical web apps; your own app may have risks the list does not cover (business-logic abuse, for example). Map each category to concrete controls in your codebase and to tests that prove the controls work.

key_points: Broken Access Control — users reaching data or actions they should not.
Cryptographic Failures — sensitive data exposed because it is not protected properly.
Injection — untrusted input treated as code or commands.
Insecure Design — security missing from the design itself, not just the code.
Security Misconfiguration — unsafe defaults, open admin panels, verbose errors.
Vulnerable and Outdated Components — known-buggy libraries left in place.
Identification and Authentication Failures — weak or broken login and session handling.
Software and Data Integrity Failures — trusting updates, plugins or data that were tampered with.
Security Logging and Monitoring Failures — attacks happening unnoticed.
Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) — the server tricked into making requests on the attacker's behalf.

defensive_examples.title: Defence in depth, not one magic fix
defensive_examples.code: Design review -> threat model -> secure defaults -> input validation -> least privilege -> logging -> tests -> patching
defensive_examples.explanation: Each category is countered by a different layer. A checklist reviewed at design time catches more than a scanner run at the end.

defensive_examples.title: Keep an inventory of your components
defensive_examples.code:
# List installed packages and check them against known issues
pip list
npm audit
# Pin versions and update on a schedule, not only after an incident
defensive_examples.explanation: You cannot patch a library you do not know you use. An inventory plus a regular update routine addresses the outdated-components category.

knowledge_check.question: Which OWASP Top 10 category covers a normal user viewing another user's private records by changing an ID in a URL?
knowledge_check.explanation: Changing an ID to reach someone else's data is an access-control failure: the app never checked whether this user was allowed to see that record.

knowledge_check.question: Why is the OWASP Top 10 a starting point rather than a complete security standard?
options: It only lists the ten most common high-impact web risks
It is only about mobile apps
knowledge_check.explanation: It ranks common risks in typical web apps. Your app can still have business-logic or platform-specific risks the list does not describe.
